THE COMPUTING BEHIND THE SPIDER

Three things that look like one.

Characters, graphemes, and glyphs belong to different layers.

01 / DATA
U+0061 + U+0301

Code points

The values that make up text. The letter “a” and its combining acute accent are two code points.

02 / GROUPING
[ á ]

Graphemes

The clusters we usually perceive as characters. That accented letter forms one grapheme.

03 / DRAWING
á

Glyphs and ink

The shapes drawn by a font. Their ink can escape its box. Counting graphemes tells you how the text groups.

What exactly are we measuring? +

Layout: The blue outline is the message's block box, measured with getBoundingClientRect(). The horizontal guide marks the first baseline using a zero-size inline element.

Ink: The browser draws the glyphs in the DOM with the selected font and overflow setting. The orange guide uses measureText() and actualBoundingBox* from Canvas to estimate ink bounds before clipping. Canvas and the DOM can differ. The guide is omitted for line breaks, tabs, and unsupported control characters.

Graphemes: The lab uses Intl.Segmenterwith the browser's Unicode version. If the API is missing, the grapheme count is unavailable.

Selection: The green outline uses each grapheme's UTF-16 offsets and Range.getClientRects(). It marks the grapheme's position and follows each view's clipping. Native highlighting, where available, keeps the text in one node. Ligatures can share geometry. Use the inspector chips to select one grapheme at a time.

Fonts: The names identify requested families. The browser can draw missing characters with fallback fonts. Mark count alone cannot predict height.

Normalization: NFC composes and NFD decomposes canonically. Repeated marks can remain in either form. U+FC5E is a presentation ligature (category Lo). Try it to compare with the original specimen.
